title: Math & Number Theory
tagline: GCD, primes, modular arithmetic, fast exponentiation — the small set of identities that turn O(n) loops into O(log n).
intro:
A surprising number of interview problems are really math problems wearing a coding costume. A few classical results — Euclid's GCD, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, binary exponentiation, and the rules of modular arithmetic — turn brute-force loops into logarithmic-time one-liners. Recognising the underlying math is the whole game; once you do, the code is short.

The recurring theme is **replacing iteration with an identity**. Computing x^n by multiplying n times is O(n); squaring repeatedly is O(log n). Testing each number for primality is O(n√n); the sieve marks all primes up to n in O(n log log n). GCD by listing divisors is slow; Euclid's algorithm is O(log min(a,b)).

This module covers GCD/LCM, prime generation and testing, modular arithmetic (and why huge answers ask for 'mod 1e9+7'), and fast exponentiation — plus the integer-overflow trap that bites in Java but not Python.
objectives: Compute GCD with Euclid's algorithm and derive LCM from it
Generate primes with the Sieve of Eratosthenes and test primality in O(√n)
Apply modular arithmetic rules and understand 'answer mod 1e9+7'
Compute powers in O(log n) with binary exponentiation
Avoid integer overflow (Java) and use Python's big ints / built-in pow
Recognise when a problem reduces to a known number-theory identity

signals: "Count / list primes up to n", primality testing
Compute x^n efficiently, or x^n mod m
Digit problems, palindromic numbers, base conversion
antiSignals: Problem is combinatorial structure, not arithmetic → DP/graph
Small fixed n where a direct loop is trivially fast
Floating point where precision matters → be careful, prefer integers

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Math problems often hide a shortcut that beats counting one step at a time. Instead of multiplying a number by itself n times, you can square it and halve the exponent over and over - a bit like doubling a recipe by doubling it again and again rather than adding one portion at a time.

Example: `2^10` equals `(2^5)^2`, and `2^5` equals `(2^2)^2 * 2`. That's only a handful of multiplications - roughly as many as it takes to halve 10 down to 1 - instead of ten separate ones. Spotting the hidden identity is what turns a slow loop into just a few quick steps.

sections.heading: The core toolkit
sections.body:
| Tool | What it does | Complexity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **GCD (Euclid)** | greatest common divisor | O(log min(a,b)) |
| **LCM** | least common multiple = `a/gcd · b` | via GCD |
| **Sieve of Eratosthenes** | all primes ≤ n | O(n log log n) |
| **Primality test** | is n prime? | O(√n) |
| **Modular arithmetic** | arithmetic under `mod m` | O(1) per op |
| **Binary exponentiation** | x^n (mod m) | O(log n) |

These six cover the overwhelming majority of math interview questions. The pattern is always the same: a clever identity collapses a linear (or worse) loop into logarithmic or near-linear time.

Match the signal to the tool:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Math problem"] --> B{"Signal?"}
  B -- "GCD / LCM / fractions" --> C["Euclid's algorithm"]
  B -- "Primes up to n" --> D["Sieve of Eratosthenes"]
  B -- "x^n or x^n mod m" --> E["Binary exponentiation"]
  B -- "Answer is huge" --> F["Work mod 1e9+7 each step"]
```

sections.heading: GCD and LCM (Euclid's algorithm)
sections.body: Euclid's insight: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`, repeating until the remainder is 0. It converges in O(log min(a,b)) steps. LCM follows directly: `lcm(a,b) = a / gcd(a,b) * b` — divide *before* multiplying to avoid overflow.

sections.heading: Primes: sieve and testing
sections.body: To **test one number** for primality, trial-divide only up to √n — if no divisor is found by then, none exists (divisors come in pairs straddling √n). To find **all primes up to n**, the Sieve of Eratosthenes is far better than testing each: mark every multiple of each prime as composite, leaving the primes unmarked, in O(n log log n).

callouts.text: Start marking multiples from p*p, not 2*p — smaller multiples were already marked by smaller primes. This is the small optimisation interviewers like to see.

sections.heading: Modular arithmetic
sections.body:
When answers grow astronomically (counting paths, combinatorics), problems ask for the result **modulo 1e9+7** (a large prime) so it fits in a 64-bit integer. The arithmetic rules let you apply the mod at every step instead of at the end:

| Operation | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Addition | `(a + b) mod m = ((a mod m) + (b mod m)) mod m` |
| Multiplication | `(a · b) mod m = ((a mod m) · (b mod m)) mod m` |
| Subtraction | `((a - b) mod m + m) mod m` (keep it non-negative) |
| Division | multiply by modular inverse (needs Fermat / ext-Euclid) |

Apply the mod after every multiply/add to keep numbers bounded — don't compute the giant number first.

callouts.text: Division does NOT distribute over mod. To divide under a modulus you multiply by the modular inverse: a / b mod p = a · b^(p-2) mod p when p is prime (Fermat's little theorem).

sections.heading: Binary (fast) exponentiation
sections.body: Computing x^n by multiplying n times is O(n). Binary exponentiation squares the base and halves the exponent: `x^n = (x^(n/2))^2`, handling the odd case with one extra multiply — O(log n). Combined with a mod at each step, it computes `x^n mod m` for huge n, which is the backbone of modular inverse and many counting problems.

codeExamples.label: Fast exponentiation (x^n mod m)
codeExamples.code:
def power(x, n, mod=10**9 + 7):
    result = 1
    x %= mod
    while n > 0:
        if n & 1:                 # odd exponent
            result = result * x % mod
        x = x * x % mod           # square the base
        n >>= 1                   # halve the exponent
    return result

# Python built-in does this: pow(x, n, mod)

interviewTalking: Spot the math underneath: "This reduces to GCD" or "The answer is huge, so they want it mod 1e9+7, and I'll apply the mod after each multiply." Show you know the efficient version: "Naive x^n is O(n), but binary exponentiation squares the base for O(log n)." Flag the language difference proactively: "In Java I'll use long and divide before multiplying for LCM to avoid overflow; Python has big integers so I'll use the built-in pow(x, n, mod)." That overflow awareness is a strong signal.
commonMistakes: Integer overflow in Java (use long, divide before multiply in LCM) — Python is immune
Trial-dividing up to n instead of √n for primality
Starting the sieve's inner loop at 2*p instead of p*p
Distributing mod over division (you need a modular inverse instead)
Negative results after modular subtraction — add m before the final mod
Computing x^n directly then modding, overflowing before the mod applies
complexityNotes: Euclid's GCD is O(log min(a,b)). Single-number primality is O(√n). Sieve of Eratosthenes is O(n log log n) time, O(n) space. Binary exponentiation is O(log n). Modular operations are O(1) each on machine words.
